title: AI prediction leads people to forgo guaranteed rewards
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether merely believing that an AI system can predict one’s behavior changes the choices people make. The authors build on Newcomb’s paradox and investigate whether AI prediction can shift decision-making toward forgoing a guaranteed reward, even when no recommendation is given and the AI’s actual predictive accuracy is not revealed. They frame this as a psychological mechanism they call “predictive binding,” in which people treat a prediction as if it partly determines what they will do.

The paper reports four preregistered online experiments with 1,305 adult participants recruited through Prolific. Study 1 compared an AI predictor with a random picker wheel in a one-shot monetary choice task. Study 2 tested robustness across interactive and non-interactive interfaces, including an LLM-based chatbot (GPT-4.1) in the AI condition. Study 3 generalized the effect to vignette scenarios about job interviews, mobile data plans, and freelancing task selection, comparing AI prediction, human-expert prediction, and no-prediction controls. Study 4 examined repeated interaction over five rounds, with the AI consistently predicting either one-boxing or two-boxing.

Across studies, participants were more likely to choose the lower-payoff option when it was framed as predicted by AI, thereby foregoing a guaranteed reward. The effect persisted across interfaces, decision contexts, and repeated exposure, even after repeated prediction failures. The authors conclude that perceived predictive authority can reshape decisions, not just forecast them, and that this influence may be self-reinforcing over time. Because the work is about general decision behavior rather than education, it does not directly address K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based large language model chatbot/assistant.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in Study 2 to support the interactive AI condition as the LLM-based chatbot. The authors state that the interactive AI condition was powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API, and ChatGPT was also used to refine the system prompt for the chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: This paper did not evaluate ChatGPT as a pedagogical tutoring or feedback tool; it used a GPT-based chatbot as a predictor in a behavioral decision task. In Study 2, the interactive AI condition used an LLM-based chatbot powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API, but the paper reports no educational outcome for ChatGPT itself. The broader finding was that AI prediction increased one-boxing relative to random framing, but that effect was about predictive authority rather than instructional coaching.
findings.measure: Choice in a Newcomb-style one-boxing task and perceived predictiveness
findings.sample_size: n=801 across Studies 1 and 2; Study 2 n=601

quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a preregistered multi-study experiment with randomized conditions and a fixed-effect meta-analysis across Studies 1 and 2, which supports strong internal validity. However, the tool use is not an educational intervention and the GPT-based system is only incidental to the study's main behavioral task.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect on one-boxing is statistically meaningful and the odds ratio is large, but it concerns a non-educational decision task rather than K–12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback. Because there is no direct evidence of educational benefit or harm, the impact on the requested topic is unclear.
